how-much-to-charge-for-spray-foam-insula.text:
Spray foam bid calculator

How much to charge for spray foam insulation

A published “$3.50 / sf of attic” special prices the floor. Residential spray foam is not the floor. It is board feet — square feet times inches — plus a closed-cell rim the coupon never counted, plus an ignition coating on exposed foam. Matching the coupon on an 8-inch open-cell attic with a rim is how a sold job becomes a drum-short loss after the first bay.

Open the free bid calculator

The number an attic-square-foot special cannot see

Take a 40×30 attic, 8 inches of open-cell, no rim, no coating. That is 1,200 square feet of plane and 9,600 board feet — 10,560 after 10% waste. The coupon says $3.50 × 1,200 = $4,200. Foam at a starting $0.55 per board foot is already $5,808 before labor. Raise the same shop to an 80-foot closed-cell rim and an intumescent coat. The attic is still “about 1,200,” so the coupon barely moves. The job did not: 185 board feet of closed-cell, coating on 1,200 square feet, and rim hours the 8-inch floor never had.

Put 5.5 inches of closed-cell on a 6/12 cathedral. Closed-cell is a different drum and a different rate. Pitch-adjusted roof area is not attic floor. $3.50 per square foot of floor is not a closed-cell price.

How to price it

  1. Measure the sprayed plane. Attic floor is length times width. Cathedral multiplies by a pitch factor.
  2. Count board feet: square feet times inches. Add rim board feet. That sum is what drums are sold in.
  3. Split open-cell and closed-cell. Hybrid is one inch closed plus open-cell fill. Waste is higher on open-cell.
  4. Price ignition coating, access, mobilization, and the permit allowance.
  5. Load the wage, add foam and coating, mark overhead on direct cost, then divide by one minus the target margin. The walk-away price is total cost.

The spray foam bid calculator does that arithmetic in the browser from your own hours and invoices. Starting cell rates, waste percents, and material rates are ballpark figures to replace, not a drum quote or a code table.

What this is not

This is not an energy-code opinion, a permit, a construction specification, a manufacturer warranty, or an engineering stamp. Confirm the jurisdiction, the assembly, and a qualified professional before sending a price. The output is arithmetic on the numbers you typed.

No warranty. This free article and calculator are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from their use.

Common questions

How much to charge for spray foam insulation?

Start from the sprayed plane, count the board feet an attic-square-foot special cannot see, then add cell type, rim-joist footage, ignition coating, waste, and the permit. A published $3.50 per square foot special only sees attic floor.

Why do board feet and rim joists change the price?

A 1,200 square-foot attic at 8 inches of open-cell is 9,600 board feet. An 80-foot rim at 9.25 inches sprayed 3 inches is another 185 board feet of closed-cell the attic coupon never counted. Matching the coupon is how the rim job loses money.

Is this an energy-code calculation?

No. Cell rates, waste percents, and hours here are common starting points on residential bids. They are not an energy-code opinion, a permit, a manufacturer warranty, or an engineering stamp.

See this calculator vs. a flat per-square-foot attic price for what the coupon method above gets wrong on a rim or a cell switch, spelled out side by side.

    Common questions

    Why is the unit board feet rather than square feet?

    Because foam is sold and yielded by volume, and thickness is the variable that moves cost most. The default attic floor is 40 × 30 ft, or 1,200 sq ft, sprayed at 8 inches — which is 1,200 × 8 = 9,600 board feet. Doubling the thickness doubles the material without touching the square footage, so a per-square-foot price is only meaningful once the depth is pinned down.

    Why does the order quantity exceed what actually gets sprayed?

    Because of the waste allowance, which defaults to 10%. The plane needs 9,600 board feet, so the estimate orders 10,560. Real losses come from overspray, trimming to depth, hose purge, and the tail of a set you cannot use — a set you paid for either way. Set the allowance to zero only if you are genuinely billing at consumed yield rather than purchased yield.

    Why is material almost nine times the labor cost?

    That is the shape of a spray foam job, and it is worth seeing plainly: on the defaults the foam and consumables come to $5,993.00 against $707.10 of labor for 16.74 hours. It means your exposure is chemical pricing and yield, not crew speed. A 10% swing in foam cost moves this bid about $600; a 10% swing in labor productivity moves it about $70.

    What R-value do the defaults actually deliver?

    About R-29.6 — 8 inches of open-cell foam at roughly R-3.7 per inch. That is the nominal centre-of-cavity figure for the product, not an assembly rating, and it does not account for framing, compression, or the air-sealing benefit that is often the real reason for the job. If you are quoting to a code minimum, check the required assembly value rather than the nominal number.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. vs-a-flat-per-square-foot-price.html.text:
← Spray Foam Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-square-foot attic price

A published “$3.50 a square foot” special multiplies one rate by attic floor and stops. This page names no company or product — it compares against that generic pricing method, and what it cannot see once the job is not the one the rate was written for.

What each approach actually does

A flat per-square-foot rate is fast: measure the attic floor, multiply by a published number, quote it. It works because it is the same arithmetic every homeowner and every competing bid uses, so it is easy to compare and easy to explain. It has one input — floor area — and treats every job at that area as the same job.

This calculator starts from the same measurement and then prices what the flat rate cannot: board feet (square feet times inches, the unit foam is actually bought and sprayed in, not floor), a pitch-adjusted cathedral area instead of flat floor, a closed-cell rim in lineal feet, an ignition coating on exposed foam, waste by cell type, tight-access hours, and the permit allowance — then loads a wage, marks overhead, and divides by one minus a target margin to print the walk-away price below which the job loses money.

JobWhat a flat rate seesWhat this calculator adds
1,200 sf attic, 8″ open-cell, no rim, no coating1,200 sf × the published rate — and for a plain floor this is close.9,600 board feet, cell-specific waste, and the same walk-away math — a check on the flat number, not a different one.
Same attic, plus an 80 lf closed-cell rim and an intumescent coatStill “about 1,200 sf” — the quote barely moves.~185 board feet of closed-cell rim the floor number never counted, plus coating hours and material on the exposed plane.
1,800 sf cathedral at 6/12 pitch, 5.5″ closed-cellPriced as if it were 1,800 sf of flat floor.Pitch-adjusted sprayed area (roof area is larger than floor area at any pitch) at the closed-cell rate, not the open-cell one.
Switching open-cell to closed-cell on the same floorNo difference — both are “spray foam” at one rate.A different drum, a different board-foot yield, and this calculator's own same-attic, three-cell comparison table.
Am I still above my own walk-away cost at the price I'm about to send?Not answered — the rate is the quote.This calculator's proposed-price check against total cost, before you send it.

Neither is wrong on a plain attic floor with one cell type, no rim, and no coating — the two can land close there, and this calculator's own same-attic comparison will show it. The gap opens on everything a flat floor rate cannot describe: a rim, a coating, a cell switch, or a pitched roof, which is most jobs that are not the one the rate was written for.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Why not just multiply attic square feet by a rate?

Because spray foam is bought and sprayed in board feet — square feet times inches — not attic floor. A flat rate written for one thickness on plain attic floor cannot see a closed-cell rim, a switch from open- to closed-cell, an ignition coating on exposed foam, or a cathedral roof's pitch-adjusted area. Two jobs that read the same on the tape measure can be a different number of board feet, a different cell mix, and a different price.

What does a flat per-square-foot rate get wrong first?

The rim. A published attic-floor rate prices the floor and stops. An 80-foot closed-cell rim at 9.25 inches sprayed 3 inches deep is roughly 185 board feet of closed-cell foam that never shows up in an attic-square-foot number, because the floor area did not change — only the board feet did. The second most common miss is cell type: open-cell and closed-cell are different drums at different rates, and a flat rate written for one silently prices the other the same.

Is a flat rate ever fine to quote from?

For a fast phone estimate on a plain attic floor with no rim, no coating, and one cell type, a flat rate and this calculator can land close. It stops matching once any of that changes — a rim, a coating, a cell switch, a cathedral pitch, or tight access — which is most jobs that are not the one the rate was written for.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you type — spans, wages, costs, or the price you send — is sent to a server.

This page names no specific company or product — it compares against the generic method of quoting attic square feet times a flat rate, not a competing calculator or platform. This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this spray-foam job cost, given its board feet, cell, and rim, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the sprayed plane, open, closed, or hybrid cell, rim-joist footage and thickness, ignition or thermal coating, waste percent, access, and the permit allowance, plus loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a same-attic three-cell comparison table, and a copyable customer-facing bid summary — plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
